stem: Monochromatic light is incident on a clean metal surface. No photoelectrons are emitted. Which change can enable emission?
options: Increase the frequency above the threshold frequency
Increase the illuminated area without changing the frequency
Increase the exposure time without changing the frequency
Increase the intensity while keeping the frequency unchanged
explanation: Each photon must individually have energy at least the work function. Raising intensity alone does not overcome a sub-threshold photon energy.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: Light of frequency above the threshold frequency illuminates a metal. The intensity is doubled without changing the frequency. What happens to the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy and the emission rate?
options: Maximum kinetic energy doubles; emission rate is unchanged
Maximum kinetic energy is unchanged; emission rate approximately doubles
explanation: Kₘₐₓ = hf − Φ depends on frequency, not intensity. Doubling intensity at fixed frequency doubles the number of photons arriving per second and usually the electron emission rate.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: A metal has work function 2.3 eV. Photons of energy 5.0 eV illuminate it. What is the maximum kinetic energy of emitted electrons?
explanation: Einstein’s equation gives Kₘₐₓ = 5.0 − 2.3 = 2.7 eV.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: The threshold wavelength of a metal is 500 nm. Light of which wavelength can produce photoelectrons from this metal?
explanation: Photon energy is hc/λ, so wavelengths at or below the threshold (500 nm) can release photoelectrons.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: Photons each have energy 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and illuminate a metal with work function 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the magnitude of the stopping potential?

stem: The same metal is illuminated with light of frequencies f and 2f, both above threshold. Which statement about the two stopping potentials is correct?
options: The second stopping potential is smaller
The second stopping potential must be exactly twice the first
explanation: eVₛ = hf − Φ, so Vₛ(2f) − Vₛ(f) = hf/e; the work function cancels.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: For one metal, stopping potential Vₛ is plotted against incident light frequency, as shown. Which property can be determined directly from the gradient of the straight line?
options: The elementary charge divided by Planck constant
The speed of light divided by elementary charge
The Planck constant divided by elementary charge
The work function multiplied by elementary charge
explanation: From eVₛ = hf − Φ, the graph gradient dVₛ/df = h/e.
diagramAlt: Straight-line graph of stopping potential versus light frequency with a positive gradient.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: The graph of maximum photoelectron kinetic energy against light frequency is a straight line. What is the magnitude of its vertical-axis intercept, when extrapolated to zero frequency?
explanation: Kₘₐₓ = hf − Φ has a y-intercept −Φ, so its magnitude is the work function.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: For a given metal, what does the threshold frequency mean?
options: The minimum frequency of incident light required to release photoelectrons from the metal
The minimum work required to release photoelectrons from the metal
The energy required to excite an electron from the ground state to the first excited state
The maximum frequency of incident light at which photoelectrons can be released from the metal
explanation: The threshold frequency is the minimum frequency of incident light capable of ejecting electrons from this metal. The minimum energy needed is the work function (Φ = hf₀), not a frequency. An atomic excitation energy relates to transitions between bound states, not emission from the metal surface.

distractor_notes.B: Confuses minimum required energy (work function) with minimum frequency.
distractor_notes.C: Confuses excitation to a bound atomic state with photoelectric emission.
distractor_notes.D: Confuses the lower frequency threshold with an upper bound.

sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: A metal is illuminated by two beams with the same number of photons arriving per second. Both frequencies exceed the threshold. The frequency increases, but photon arrival rate remains fixed. In an ideal photoelectric experiment, how do the saturation current and stopping potential change?
options: Saturation current increases; stopping potential increases
Saturation current is unchanged; stopping potential increases
Saturation current decreases; stopping potential increases
Saturation current is unchanged; stopping potential decreases
explanation: Saturation current is set by the electron rate (same photon arrival rate, assuming identical quantum efficiency), whereas Vₛ increases because Kₘₐₓ = hf − Φ increases.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: Electron diffraction from a crystal is evidence that electrons
options: behave as waves under suitable conditions
are emitted only at particular frequencies
explanation: Diffraction and interference are wave phenomena; electrons demonstrate wave-like behaviour.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: What is the correct de Broglie relation for a particle with momentum p?
explanation: The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: A non-relativistic particle has its speed doubled while its mass stays constant. What happens to its de Broglie wavelength?
explanation: Since p=mv, λ=h/(mv). Doubling v halves the wavelength.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: Two non-relativistic particles have the same kinetic energy. Particle B has four times the mass of particle A. What is the de Broglie wavelength of particle B divided by the de Broglie wavelength of particle A?
explanation: λ=h/√(2mK). With equal K, λ∝1/√m; a fourfold mass makes λ half as large.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference V. The accelerating voltage is increased to 9V. What is the ratio of the new de Broglie wavelength to the original?
explanation: Non-relativistically, p=√(2meV) and λ∝V⁻¹ᐟ². Tripling the momentum reduces λ by a factor of 3.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: An electron is accelerated from rest through 150 V. Its de Broglie wavelength is closest to which value?
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: A beam of electrons is diffracted by a crystal. The electrons are then accelerated through a larger potential difference before reaching the same crystal. What happens to the angular separation between diffraction maxima?
options: It decreases because their de Broglie wavelength decreases
It remains unchanged because the crystal spacing is fixed
It becomes zero for every higher voltage
It increases because electrons have more energy
explanation: Greater accelerating voltage produces greater electron momentum and smaller λ, so the characteristic diffraction angles become smaller.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: For a matter-wave diffraction experiment, which change makes diffraction effects more noticeable?
options: Increase particle mass at the same speed while keeping the slit fixed
Use a narrower slit, with the same particle momentum
Use a wider slit, with the same particle momentum
Increase particle momentum while keeping the slit width fixed
explanation: Diffraction broadening is more evident when slit width is comparable to λ; decreasing the width increases diffraction angle.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: Electrons of de Broglie wavelength 0.20 nm pass through two slits separated by 0.10 mm. A screen is 2.0 m from the slits. What is the approximate fringe spacing? Assume small angles.

stem: Electrons travel through a double-slit arrangement, producing an interference pattern on a screen, as shown. If electron momentum doubles while the geometry is unchanged, what happens to the fringe spacing?
options: It is one quarter of its original value
explanation: Fringe spacing is proportional to wavelength, and λ=h/p. Doubling p halves λ and the fringe spacing.
diagramAlt: Simple electron-beam double-slit diagram with two slits, a distant screen and diverging paths.

stem: During Compton scattering from an electron initially at rest, an X-ray photon is scattered through a non-zero angle. Which statement is correct?
options: The scattered photon has a longer wavelength
The photon and electron each conserve their own momentum
The scattered photon has a shorter wavelength
The scattered photon has gained energy
explanation: Compton shift Δλ=h(1−cosθ)/(mₑc) is positive for non-zero scattering angles; photon energy hc/λ falls.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: For Compton scattering by an initially stationary electron, at which photon scattering angle is the wavelength shift greatest?
explanation: Δλ=(h/mₑc)(1−cosθ) is maximized when cosθ=−1, that is θ=180°.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: An X-ray photon is Compton-scattered through 90° by an electron initially at rest. What is the approximate increase in photon wavelength?
explanation: At 90°, cosθ=0, so Δλ=(h/mₑc)=2.43 pm.
sourceNote: Original question aligned with IB Physics guide first assessment 2025 E.2; uploaded exam questions used only as style and difficulty benchmarks.

stem: An incident photon has wavelength 80.0 pm. After Compton scattering, its wavelength is 82.0 pm. Approximately what fraction of the incident photon energy has been transferred to the electron?
explanation: Transferred fraction =1−Eₑ/Eᵢ=1−(λᵢ/λf)=1−80/82≈0.0244=2.4%.
